prediction:
THOUGHT: The history of exertional right calf cramps that reliably subside with brief rest is classic for intermittent claudication from arterial insufficiency rather than a neurogenic back cause. The patient has multiple vascular risk factors (longstanding type 2 diabetes, heavy tobacco use, hypertension, elevated fasting glucose and HbA1c). On exam the right pedal pulses are absent and straight-leg-raise provokes pallor and tingling in the foot—elevation-induced pallor/paresthesia supports an arterial (ischemic) mechanism. Neurologic testing shows normal strength and no focal sensory loss, making a compressive radiculopathy less likely. Definitive vascular imaging (Doppler) demonstrates significant femoropopliteal artery stenosis in the right leg, which anatomically explains the symptoms. Altogether these findings indicate atherosclerotic peripheral arterial disease of the right lower extremity manifesting as intermittent claudication and ischemic paresthesia.

DIAGNOSIS: Peripheral arterial disease of the right lower extremity due to femoropopliteal atherosclerotic stenosis (intermittent claudication).
